newsitem.title: BRAZIL: US aluminium can output seen rising 2.0 pct a year.
newsitem.headline: US aluminium can output seen rising 2.0 pct a year.

text.p: Production of aluminium cans in the U.S. should rise two percent throughout the decade from last year's 100.7 billion units, the president of IMCO Recycling Inc told a Brazilian aluminium recycling conference.
Total global can shipments are projected to rise about five percent annually to a total of 210 billion units by 2000, said Richard Kerr, who is also a director of U.S. Aluminium Association.

Aluminium use in car parts is probably the most promisiing market for aluminium in the future, he said, with analysts expecting usage to rise to 350 lbs (157.5 kgs) per vehicle by 2000 from 250 lbs (112.5 kgs) in 1996.
Some analysts say this figure could be even closer to 500 lbs (225 kgs), he said.
U.S. aluminium consumption is expected to increase modestly through to the end of the decade, rising to about 24 billion lbs (10.8 million tonnnes) from 21 billion (9.45 million) in 1995.
This represents an annual growth rate of almost three percent and is close to the anticipated rise in GDP, he said.

The majority of the increase in overall aluminium consumption will be supplied by recycled metal, total production of which is expected to grow to nine billion lbs (4.05 million tonnes) in 2000 from seven billion (3.15 million) in 1995, an annual growth rate of about five percent.
Imco's annual capacity in 1996 will be at least 1.7 billion lbs (765,000 tonnes) and the firm is expecting output to grow at at least 20 percent per year, Kerr said.
"By the year 2000 we expect to be twice the size we were in 1995," Kerr said.
In November 1995, Imco put 1995 aluminium production capacity at 453,600 tonnes.
Aluminium consumption in Brazil is increasing rapidly, having risen so far eight percent from 1995, mainly due to the the fast-growing beverage-can market, Kerr said.
Aluminium cans in Brazil are expected to increase sharply their share of the beverage packaging market which now stands at less than 10 percent.

Brazil's can recycling rate is now at the high level of 63 percent, Kerr said, attributing most of this to Reynolds Metals, the U.S. aluminium producer and fabricator, whose Brazilian affiliate is Latas de Aluminio S.A. Latasa.
